purpose: Machine-facing subdomain node of a knowledge-searcher meta-KB: where and how to find, retrieve, evaluate, and synthesize authoritative applied- and computational-linguistics knowledge as concrete, evaluable work units spanning language acquisition, pedagogy, translation/interpretation/localization, tokenization, parsing, language models, corpus linguistics, and annotation.
assumptions: no observed dataset or benchmark evidence supplied; all scores are heuristic priors
covers both applied (L1/L2 acquisition, pedagogy, translation/interpretation/localization) and computational (tokenization, parsing, language models, corpus linguistics, annotation) linguistics
nodes are concrete work-units bounded to one heavy reasoning session
this KB composes the how-LLMs-work specialist on the computational/NLP side
exclusions: theoretical-only formal grammar debates without an applied/computational work unit
general machine-learning infrastructure not specific to language
non-linguistic information retrieval covered by sibling KBs

evidence_label_policy.rationale: no observed dataset or experimental evidence supplied; all estimates are heuristic priors

source_registry.description: Heuristic priors from applied and computational linguistics practice (incl. Jurafsky & Martin 'Speech and Language Processing'; Crystal 'The Cambridge Encyclopedia of Language') without an observed dataset.
supports: heuristic estimates for metrics, weights, risks, priorities, and relations
grounding_limits: not a substitute for measured evaluation

nodes.definition: Define the applied/computational-linguistics question, language(s), register, modality, success metric, and search/evaluate/synthesize objective before any method or tool choice.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: target language, register, or downstream consumer changes

pros.claim: Bounds method choice so corpus, model, and annotation work are scoped to the real question
pros.example: fix WER vs BLEU vs human-adequacy target before picking an MT vs ASR pipeline

cons.claim: Over-specification can exclude viable cross-lingual approaches early
cons.example: locking monolingual scope before testing multilingual transfer

failure_modes: mis-scoped metric optimizes the wrong linguistic objective
ignoring dialect/register variation in the target population
acceptance_tests: task spec names language(s), register, modality, metric, and search objective
reviewer confirms metric matches the applied or research goal
revisit_triggers: new downstream consumer of the output

nodes.definition: Locate and inventory authoritative language resources (corpora, lexicons, treebanks, dictionaries, parallel data, pretrained models) for the target language and task.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a new corpus/treebank/model release covers a prior gap

pros.claim: Surfaces existing high-quality resources so teams reuse rather than rebuild annotation
pros.example: find a UD treebank + license before commissioning new parsing data

cons.claim: Resource coverage for low-resource languages is sparse and uneven
cons.example: no treebank exists for the target dialect, forcing fallback

failure_modes: missing low-resource coverage silently degrades downstream

nodes.definition: Design a corpus: define population, sampling frame, balance/representativeness, size, and metadata so downstream linguistic claims generalize.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: register/genre balance is shown unrepresentative of the target population

pros.claim: Representative sampling lets corpus-derived frequencies and patterns generalize
pros.example: balance genres so collocation stats are not skewed by news text

cons.claim: True representativeness is unattainable; balance is always a judgment call
cons.example: 'balanced' corpus still over-represents written formal register

failure_modes: convenience sampling biases all downstream frequency claims
acceptance_tests: sampling frame and balance criteria documented and justified
metadata schema captures register, genre, source, date

nodes.definition: Segment raw text/speech into tokens, words, morphemes, or subwords appropriate to the language's orthography and the downstream model.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: switching to a language with different segmentation (e.g. CJK, agglutinative)

pros.claim: Correct segmentation is prerequisite for parsing, modeling, and frequency counts
pros.example: use subword BPE for morphologically rich Turkish vs whitespace for English

cons.claim: Subword schemes can fracture meaningful morphemes and hurt interpretability
cons.example: BPE splits a lemma so morphological analysis becomes noisy

failure_modes: whitespace tokenization fails on scriptio-continua languages
revisit_triggers: new target language with different orthography

nodes.definition: Design annotation scheme, label set, and guidelines (POS, syntax, semantics, discourse, NER) with adjudication rules for consistent labeling.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: theory choice (e.g. UD vs SUD) or label set is revised

pros.claim: Clear guidelines drive inter-annotator agreement and reusable gold data
pros.example: UD POS guidelines let two annotators agree on PROPN vs NOUN

cons.claim: Scheme commits to a linguistic theory that may not fit later tasks
cons.example: Penn Treebank tags lock English-specific assumptions

failure_modes: theory mismatch makes gold data non-reusable
acceptance_tests: guidelines define every label with positive and negative examples
pilot annotation reaches agreement target before scale-up

nodes.definition: Measure annotation reliability (kappa, alpha), adjudicate disagreements, and certify gold-standard data quality before it grounds models or claims.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: agreement metric drops below the certification threshold

pros.claim: Quantified agreement separates reliable gold data from noisy labels
pros.example: Cohen kappa 0.8 certifies NER spans as model-grade gold

cons.claim: High kappa can mask systematic shared bias between annotators
cons.example: both annotators apply the same wrong convention, inflating agreement

failure_modes: low agreement silently propagates label noise into models
chance-corrected metric misread as raw percent agreement
acceptance_tests: agreement computed with a chance-corrected metric and reported with CI
disagreements adjudicated and logged in an error taxonomy

nodes.definition: Analyze word structure: lemmatization, stemming, morphological tagging, and finite-state morphology for the target language.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: target language morphology type changes (fusional vs agglutinative)

pros.claim: Lemmatization normalizes inflection so frequency and retrieval count word types correctly
pros.example: map running/ran to lemma run for corpus frequency

cons.claim: Stemming over-conflates distinct lemmas and loses meaning
cons.example: Porter stemmer maps 'university' and 'universe' together

failure_modes: analyzer coverage gaps drop rare inflections

nodes.definition: Assign syntactic structure: POS tagging, dependency or constituency parsing, against an explicit grammar/treebank standard.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: treebank standard (UD version) or grammar formalism changes

pros.claim: Dependency structure enables relation extraction, grammar checking, and linguistic queries
pros.example: LAS-evaluated UD parse drives subject-verb agreement checking

cons.claim: Parser errors cascade into every downstream syntactic feature
cons.example: wrong attachment flips the semantic role of a phrase

revisit_triggers: parser accuracy drops on new domain

nodes.definition: Model meaning: word-sense disambiguation, semantic roles, coreference, and pragmatic/discourse structure beyond surface syntax.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: sense inventory or discourse framework is revised

pros.claim: Sense and role analysis lets retrieval and synthesis reason about meaning not strings
pros.example: resolve 'bank' sense before answering a finance query

cons.claim: Semantic frameworks disagree and ground truth is contested
cons.example: FrameNet vs PropBank roles label the same sentence differently

failure_modes: sense inventory mismatch breaks WSD reuse

nodes.definition: Train, adapt, or select language models (n-gram, neural, transformer) for the linguistic task, including evaluation against held-out gold.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: base model, training data, or metric definition changes

pros.claim: Modern LMs give strong baselines for tagging, parsing, MT, and generation
pros.example: fine-tune a multilingual transformer for low-resource NER

cons.claim: LMs encode training-data bias and hallucinate, masking linguistic errors
cons.example: model fluent output hides a grammatical error in agreement

failure_modes: distribution shift degrades the model silently in production
acceptance_tests: model evaluated on a leakage-checked held-out gold set
model card documents data, metric, and known failure modes
revisit_triggers: base model or training data changes

nodes.definition: Build or apply translation, post-editing, and localization pipelines; manage adequacy, fluency, terminology, and locale adaptation.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: language pair, domain terminology, or locale requirements change

pros.claim: MT plus human post-editing scales multilingual content with controlled quality
pros.example: post-edit MT draft for legal docs with locked terminology

cons.claim: Fluent MT can produce confident adequacy errors that pass casual review
cons.example: output reads fluently but inverts a negation

failure_modes: terminology drift produces inconsistent localized output
adequacy errors hidden by surface fluency

nodes.definition: Handle spoken-language work: ASR, speech-to-text, interpretation support, prosody, and real-time constraints.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: acoustic domain, accent set, or latency budget changes

pros.claim: ASR plus glossary support enables searchable speech and live interpretation aids
pros.example: WER-evaluated ASR transcribes interviews for corpus search

cons.claim: ASR error rates spike on accents, code-switching, and noisy audio
cons.example: accented speech yields garbled transcript that misleads search

nodes.definition: Model and support first- and second-language acquisition: developmental stages, transfer, interlanguage, and learner-error patterns.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: learner population, L1 background, or proficiency framework changes

pros.claim: Modeling interlanguage and transfer targets feedback to real learner errors
pros.example: predict article errors for L1-Russian learners of English

cons.claim: Acquisition theories conflict and individual variation is large
cons.example: developmental-order claims fail to predict a given learner

failure_modes: over-generalized error model misdiagnoses learner needs
ignoring L1 transfer mislabels systematic errors as random

nodes.definition: Design language teaching, curriculum, and assessment: CEFR alignment, task-based learning, and valid proficiency testing.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: proficiency standard (CEFR) or assessment policy changes

pros.claim: Standards-aligned assessment makes proficiency claims comparable and fair
pros.example: map a placement test to CEFR B1 with validated descriptors

cons.claim: Test validity and washback are hard to establish and easy to overstate
cons.example: high-stakes test measures test-taking not proficiency

nodes.definition: Query corpora: concordancing, collocation, frequency analysis, and keyword extraction to find and evaluate linguistic evidence.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: corpus version or annotation layer changes invalidate prior queries

pros.claim: Concordancing surfaces authentic usage evidence to ground linguistic claims
pros.example: collocation of 'strong' vs 'powerful' from a balanced corpus

cons.claim: Raw frequency without normalization misleads cross-corpus comparison
cons.example: comparing counts across corpora of different sizes

failure_modes: query over wrong annotation layer returns spurious hits

nodes.definition: Define metrics and benchmarks (BLEU, WER, LAS, F1, human adequacy), control for leakage, and produce comparable, calibrated evaluations.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: metric definition, benchmark version, or gold set changes

pros.claim: Calibrated, leakage-checked evaluation makes system claims trustworthy and comparable
pros.example: report BLEU with confidence intervals and a held-out test set

cons.claim: Single automatic metrics correlate weakly with real quality
cons.example: high BLEU yet poor human-judged adequacy

acceptance_tests: evaluation uses a leakage-checked held-out set and reports uncertainty
at least one human or task-grounded metric complements automatic ones

nodes.definition: Assess and mitigate linguistic bias, dialect/variety discrimination, representation harms, and ethical/consent issues in language data and models.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: new evidence of dialect, gender, or representational harm emerges

pros.claim: Bias auditing prevents systems from disadvantaging dialects and minority varieties
pros.example: audit ASR for higher WER on a stigmatized dialect

cons.claim: Bias is multi-dimensional; mitigating one axis can worsen another
cons.example: de-biasing gender terms degrades a valid domain distinction

failure_modes: consent gaps in scraped language data create legal/ethical risk
acceptance_tests: bias audit covers dialect/variety, demographic, and representational axes
consent and licensing of language data are documented

nodes.definition: Locate, triage, and credibility-rank authoritative linguistic-knowledge sources (handbooks, treebank docs, ACL/LSA literature, standards) for a query.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: authoritative standard, edition, or consensus in the field updates

pros.claim: Source triage routes queries to authoritative references over folk-linguistic claims
pros.example: prefer Jurafsky&Martin and ACL papers over a forum post for parsing

cons.claim: Authority signals lag fast-moving NLP subfields
cons.example: a superseded preprint still ranks high by citation inertia

revisit_triggers: new edition of a key reference released

nodes.definition: Integrate findings across applied and computational evidence into a calibrated, traceable answer with explicit uncertainty and provenance.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a source is retracted, superseded, or contradicted by stronger evidence

pros.claim: Traceable synthesis ties every claim to a source and an uncertainty level
pros.example: answer cites the treebank standard and flags low-resource caveats

cons.claim: Synthesis can over-smooth genuine disagreement across linguistic frameworks
cons.example: blending UD and constituency claims hides a real formalism conflict

failure_modes: unsourced claim slips into the synthesis
conflicting evidence averaged instead of surfaced
acceptance_tests: every claim links to a source and a confidence level
conflicts between sources are surfaced not silently merged

nodes.definition: Package the applied/computational-linguistics workflow for reproducibility: versioned data, seeds, configs, and a release/handoff artifact.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: data version, dependency, or license terms change

pros.claim: Versioned, seeded pipelines let results be reproduced and audited later
pros.example: pin tokenizer, model, and corpus versions in a release bundle

cons.claim: Full reproducibility is costly and often deprioritized under deadline
cons.example: unpinned dependency makes last quarter's results unrecoverable

conflict_axes.trigger: Optimizing fluent output while adequacy is under-measured
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: Human adequacy judgment overrides automatic fluency scores when they disagree.
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: escalate when fluent output reverses meaning
conflict_axes.example: fluency_vs_adequacy tradeoff arises in a real run

conflict_axes.trigger: Scaling data faster than annotation quality can be certified
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: Gold-quality threshold gates data scale-up; quality dominates quantity.
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: escalate when agreement falls below the certification threshold
conflict_axes.example: data_quantity_vs_annotation_quality tradeoff arises in a real run

conflict_axes.dominance_logic: When morphological analysis is the goal, morpheme-aware segmentation dominates.
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: escalate when analyzer coverage drops sharply
conflict_axes.example: subword_efficiency_vs_morpheme_fidelity tradeoff arises in a real run

conflict_axes.dominance_logic: Task scope caps corpus ambition; record the representativeness tradeoff.
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: escalate when scope cut threatens validity
conflict_axes.example: representativeness_vs_task_scope tradeoff arises in a real run

conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: escalate when a variety shows materially worse quality
conflict_axes.example: fairness_vs_aggregate_performance tradeoff arises in a real run

conflict_axes.trigger: Automatic metrics diverge from human/gold judgment
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: Human/gold judgment overrides a single automatic metric for high-stakes claims.
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: escalate when metric-human correlation is low
conflict_axes.example: automatic_metric_vs_human_judgment tradeoff arises in a real run

conflict_axes.trigger: A linguistic-theory choice locks reusability of gold data
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: Prefer widely-adopted standards (e.g. UD) unless task requires a specific theory.
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: escalate when downstream reuse is blocked
conflict_axes.example: theory_commitment_vs_reusability tradeoff arises in a real run

conflict_axes.trigger: A cleaner narrative pressures out necessary caveats
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: Required ethics/uncertainty caveats override a more readable but overconfident answer.
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: escalate when omitting a caveat would mislead
conflict_axes.example: synthesis_completeness_vs_caution tradeoff arises in a real run
